Campaign/Campaign-Premise.title: Campaign Premise
Campaign/Campaign-Premise.content:
To my esteemed friends,
After an extensive search of ancient tome and family records I have come across the secret to our fortune. A tenuous ancestral connection has given me title to lands near the Shallow Sea, deep in the Shrinelands. I suspect that in such untamed lands title means little, which is why I seek your aid to claim this stronghold. Towards this I would call upon our friendship and offer as a boon each of you a share of one-tenth the title.
More important than any mere legality is what I have found of arcane practicality. A record of pass phrases and perils of nearly all twenty-seven levels. With this in hand we will surely lay claim to…
THE TOWER OF MADNESS

Shrinelands V: The Tower of Madness will be a sword and sorcery campaign. Characters will be associates of Kelmos, distant descendant of the Tower Mage and minor scholar.
At some point in the past Kelmos has come to your aid from some dire and unforeseen circumstances, consider this when formulating your backstory - and now he calls upon you in return.

Game-Rules/Adventuring/Adventure.title: Adventure
Game-Rules/Adventuring/Adventure.content:
Adventurers travelling through dangerous of unknown terrain face all manner of perils. During these periods time is tracked day by day as events unfold.
Each day is generally divided into 6 watches, based on the cycles of the Red Moon. These define three periods during which the moon is visible, since it rises thrice each day, and three during which the moon is not in the sky.
A typical day consists of two watches of hiking, two watches for sleep, one for keeping camp, and another for any additional activities - detailed below. Each day use the travel procedure to determine what events unfold.
Watch Activities
Travel
During the day adventurers choose their direction of travel, selecting which hex to enter next. Upon entering a hex they learn the general terrain, encounter any obvious features of the hex, and have a distant overview of the terrain of surrounding hexes.

































TerrainTravelRoad2 / watchPlains2 / watchForest1 / watchSwamp0.5 / watchMountain0.5* / watchPoor Weather+1 difficulty
Travel in good terrain
Make Camp
One watch per day is spent making camp, eating meals, keeping watch, and performing upkeep. It is during this period that alchemists maintain their preservations, and other travel roles convey the benefits of their expertise.
If for some reason travelers are prevented from making camp then attempts to rest are automatically difficult. Alchemical substances will degrade, the following day travelers will not benefit from their specialized roles, and appropriate watches are not set. At least two travelers must make camp, otherwise any nighttime encounters automatically catch them by surprise.
Rest
Travelers must rest for at least two watches per day. Doing so requires a place which is warm, dry, sheltered from the elements, and, ideally, safe. Each element of this which is missing causes sleep to be more difficult.

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.title: Character Creation
Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content:
Creating a character requires generating the basic abilities of your adventurer, understanding their cultural and upbringings, choosing a class, defining their allies, and preparing for adventure.
During character creation you may accrue blessings of Chaos for embracing serendipity, keep track of the total number of these. At the end of character creation each will influence their life in interesting ways.

Roll characteristics
Culture
Background
Class
Class kit
Starting gear
Hit points
Name, backstory

Roll Characteristics
Characters have six Characteristics: Strength, Dexterity, Constitution, Wisdom, Intelligence, and Charisma - usually between 3 and 18.  These reflect their general potency in a number of domains.

Strength: melee attack and damage rolls, carrying capacity
Dexterity: armor class, ranged attack rolls, avoiding fireballs
Constitution: hit points, saves against poison and transformation effects
Intelligence: soul points, bonus training points
Wisdom: saves against mental and magical effects, avoiding surprise and ambush, teaching
Charisma: reaction rolls, Command Capacity

Roll a set of 3d6 four times in a row and write down these numbers. From here you have a choice:

Roll two more sets of 3d6, assign each of these six numbers to your six characteristics in any order, gain 2 blessings of Chaos.
Ignore the prior rolls and use a static array. Assign 15, 12, 10, 10, 9, 7 to your characteristics.

Each has a corresponding modifier, a derived value used when that attribute is relevant to a die roll.





































CharacteristicModifier1-2-33-5-26-8-19-11+012-14+115-17+218 or more+3
Culture and Background

Gain 2 training points in each of your culture’s favored skills,  these will be used to determine your total Skill Rank later, write down any (specializations) from cultural skills
Write down your starting languages
Note any additional traits
Determine your character’s exact birthplace from the options presented, either by roll or choice. This also includes the location on the map.

After this you may either choose your character’s background, or roll on your culture’s background chart to gain another blessing of Chaos. Note down how your character was raised and what skills they gain from this. This does not have to favor one parent or another, and can also include induction into a fraternal guild, adoption by another clan, or other manner of relationship.

Languages: Noctian
2 training points in Beastmastery, Heal, Seneschal, Alteration
Head of a heraldic animal
Born in 1d4: 1 - the domain of grand Chimericon under Prince Cyrus <x, y, z>

These kingdoms are a contentious group of fiefdoms held together by a rigid caste system, where people have the heads of animals. Long ago the people of the Beast Kingdoms lived deep within Noctis Labyrinthus, until the coming of ash and the death of the Fates drove them out. What remains in Noctis are only strange and twisted beasts.
The princes hold near absolute power within their domains, and life is harshly dictated by numerous taboos; forbidden the eating of certain foods, forbidding the use of many colors of dress by the lower classes, and circumscribing life on all fronts.
Covered more in Secrets of the Beast Kingdoms.
Alcheran

Languages: Alcheran, Psuedophidian
2 training points in Athletics, Artisanry, Diplomacy, Trade
Gain 6 points in Background skills instead of the normal 5
Born in 1d4: 1 - the vast halls of Labyrinth, 2 - the hinterlands beyond Labyrinth, 3 - the former glory of the City of Glass, 4 - a smaller city state who’s nature you help determine with your GM

Alcherans pride themselves on the democratic lineage of their city-states, where citizenship is granted to those who excel at a city’s chosen form of artisanry. Within Labyrinth the creation of books is of uptmost importance, as exemplified by the grand temple to Heron atop the acropolis.

New Lankh

Languages: Mortanian, Psuedophidian
2 training points in Alchemy, Devicecraft, Stealth, Exotic Arms
Maintenance of cost of Lankh technology is reduced by 1

New Lankh is a soot-filled city which teleported from the Wandering Moon twenty years ago, home to technological marvels that are slowly breaking down in their new environment. Previously Lankh was merely a district of a sprawling gaslit metropolis, ruled by vampiric overlords. Now its position in an entirely new world is much more uncertain.
Blemmyes

Languages: Blem, Ophidian
2 training points in Bushcraft, Heal, Lore, Investigation
Headless: 50% chance for any critical hit to be a regular hit instead

Headless men, also called the akephaloi, they have large faces on their chests rather than the typical arrangement. Most live in and around Blem, although some have migrated through Alcheran lands. The Blemmyes claim descent from the original inhabitants of the Shrinelands, having survived the floods of the First Age, corrupting sands of the Third Age, and all number of wars, plagues, and disasters.
Ophidian

Languages: Ophidian, Psuedophidian
2 training points in Alchemy, Diplomacy, Language, Seneschal
Toxic blood, ability to draw out poison

The height of the Ophidian Empire has long gone, and recent years have added further strife. Civil wars rage across what was once the empire, resulting in a small group of Ophidian refugees forming a sister city to Blem. Ophidians themselves have a varying degree of serpentine traits. Most slither on a serpentine tail, while all of them have poison blood and fangs.
City of Miners

Languages: Underspeech, Alcheran
2 training points in Artisanry, Devicecraft, Hand Weapon (Hammer), Enchantment, Mining
Cave sense: able to navigate in enclosed stone environments without light

The City of Miners has a distinct history harkening back to dwarven holds from long ago. From this they still retain their traditions, and the ability to thrive underground. In the time since they have become more akin to their Alcheran neighbors as one of the great city-states.
Xanthian

Languages: Xanthian, Psuedophidian
2 training points in Archery, Athletics, Sail, Teach
Specializations in Archery (Great Bow), Athletics (Swim), and Conjuration (Illusion)
Gain 1 additional hit point per hit die

Easternmost of the eras after atlantis#todo
The storm-hardened shores of Xanthe are home to lands of incredible abundance. Along these live the Xanthe, peerless sailors and travelers. They live in wandering clan-ships, variously warring with rivals or marrying friends. Greatest among them are their elders, those who have survived a terrible transformation to become guides for their people - however in recent times a corrupt king has taken power of exiled many of the formerly esteemed elders. The Xanthe who have ended up in the Shrinelands have a more tragic history, as the remnants of a shipwrecked expedition stranded by a formidable storm.
Distant Realm

Languages: native language of your homeland
2 training points in any 4 distinct skills, of which 2 must be General skills
+2 to a single ability score (maximum 18) reflecting the special nature of your original homeland

You are from a far distant realm, one unknown to most people of the Shrinelands. Possibly even from another plane of existence, such interlopers are common in land of Noachis and often find themselves drawn to adventure in these western lands. Work with the GM to come up with the exact nature of this origin.
Choose one of the above cultures for where your recent primary residence has been, write this down alongside some details of your original homeland. Decide if you have arrived alone, in which case you live with some form of adopted family or community, or if a small enclave of your people have joined the Shrinelands.
Time of Birth
The adventure begins in the year 320. Choose what year your character was born in, and the wind that presided over their birth. For those born in a “short year”, anytime between the year 300 and 278, these are:

Zephyrus, law season, a temperate season with many festivals
Boreas, monsoon season, a time of potent storms and torrential rain
Eurus, chaos season, the most powerful season of vibrant growth and unprecedented change
Notus, dry season, a dangerous time of oppressive heat and war

For those born in the year 301 or after their birth occurred during a long year. This is the result of the Wandering Moon, a sister planet which arrives every 22 years. Each convergence results in an alteration between short years and long years. Long years proceed slower, having more days and an additional season: a cold and cursed time called Winter - the still season.
Class
Choose what class your character is.
The classes are fighting-men, men of many ways, and magic-users. Fighting-Men are masters at arms, and able to lead with great skill. Men of Many Ways gain specializations in all of their skills, and oft find themselves protected by good fortune. Although any dedicated practitioner can learn some sorcery, Magic-Users have a natural affinity for the arcane. Alternatively you may choose two half-classes, as detailed under the rules for Dual-Class characters.
For your class write down

Starting HP, this is the maximum value on the HD + Constitution modifier
Saving throws, Evasion includes Dexterity modifier, mental includes Wisdom modifier, physical includes Constitution modifier
Special abilities for your class

Additionally your characters have had some time as adventurers to gain a variety of skills. For the specific classes you gain. Alternatively you may choose a preset Class Kits for a character with more specific training.

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.title: Secrets of Blem
Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content:
If asked the blemmyes will explain that their progenitor was sentenced to death for a terrible affront against the gods. But when the headsman came to issue the punishment he simply tucked in his head, causing the headsman to miss. And thus he and his descendants no longer have heads to lose. Since then the ongoing displeasure of fickle gods has put them through all manner of trials - each of which they survive with the same optimistic determination.
Many Alcherans claim Blem is the secret City of Poison, a treacherous place reviled for its insidious treatment of guests. In recent times Ophidian refugees arriving at Blem have decided to embrace this dire rumor.
Very few are permitted within the Beast Kingdoms, as they are distrusted as a result of their immunity to their ritual of changing.

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.title: Secrets of New Lankh
Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content:
The city of New Lankh did not exist until twenty years ago. During the last conjunction of the Wandering Moon the community appeared in its current location. Although astronomers had long been aware that the Wandering Moon was not merely a celestial body, but another world populated by its own people, the sudden proof of this still came as a shock to the Shrinelands.
Before its teleportation New Lankh was a district of Lankh, grand capitol of Mortania. Now it occupies an uneasy position in the politics of the Shrinelands, caught between the rivalry of Hapolis and Chimericon.
The city itself is a sooty dark labyrinth due to a spell that prevents wind from entering the city. Primarily this is useful as many of the alchemical and mechanical innovations which the city depends upon are thwarted by exposure to the various winds of the Shrinelands; however many speculate that secret forces in the city have their own reasons for maintaining it as a dark and insular sanctuary.
Amongst these inventions include numerous marvels unheard of to the rest of the world. Pipes direct the flow of energetic liquids which create gateways of force and flame. Foundries create potent metals which retain greater strength and sharpness. Clockwork controls sluice gates and other marvels are commonplace within this shadowed city.


                  
                  New Lankh Story Seeds 
                  
                

A close associate was part of a cell of saboteurs attempting to destroy the Dome of Preservation, or a member of the Watch who caught them. Possibly both simultaneously.
Numerous flux barriers block the lower sections of the city, but in the depths is great wealth for those bold enough to seek it.

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.title: Secrets of Xanthe
Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content:
Most peculiar is that they are guides by the wisdom of “elders.” Late in their lives Xanthe fall into a terrible comatose fever, often resulting in death. Those who survive are radically reshaped, both in mind and body. Strong, near perfect memory, totally sexless, and able to survive on rations that would starve any other man. Alongside this their minds have an inevitable focus on the larger picture - for the good of all peoples. As such elders form a caste of aesthetics, who renounce worldly goods to instead guide and teach a younger generation.
Descendants of Atlantis

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.title: Secrets of the Beast Kingdoms
Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content:
Chimericon <11,28> is the largest of the kingdoms of the Beast Kingdoms, however half a dozen other princes rule outlying holdings that range from small settlements to moderate castles. Within these there are rigid castes composed of the various orders of beasts. Princes and other high nobles supersede even this system, often changing forms based on fashion or whim. At the low end are the dog-men and other ignoble creatures, at the highest end fashion dictates what forms are adopted. Your form likely reflects your family occupation.
Most princes employ wizard-priests as court advisors. Among their most important duties are maintaining the health of their liege lords, and applying the rituals required to grant animal aspects to the people of the Beast Kingdoms.
Notable Characters

Prince Cyrus - leader of Chimericon and most powerful of the princes, known for a short temper and as a skilled duelist
Prince Hystaspes of Altercon - ailing prince of the westernmost holding, suspected to be a puppet of his advisors
Prince Darius of Sulicon - one of the lesser princes, notable for having married an important noble from New Lankh in an effort to secure an alliance
Broach the Marvelous - court wizard of Darius, and one of the more potent wizards of the western Shrinelands, known for his eccentric habits
Asterion Bicameral - bull-headed leader of a rogue sect of Asterion, charismatic, bold, and hated by Hapolis
Xeren - high priest of the Western Wind and key advisor to Chimericon, notable for his vehement opposition to the will of She-Who-Lurks



                  
                  Conflicts of the Beast Kingdoms 
                  
                

A family member was sentenced to death by being exiled to the Isle of the Chimera after having displeased Prince Cyrus

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content:
Trained in the style of alchemy familiar to Mortania.
Initiate: May make royal glue, smoke bombs, firebombs, bitebane, and black ichor from memory, without needing to consume a formula.

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.title: Armsmaster
Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content: You are exceptionally deadly in armed combat. Add your skill rank to damage with melee weapons.

Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.title: Animal Aspect
Game-Rules/Classes-and-Character-Creatio.content:
You or an ancestor has undergone the Ritual of Becoming gaining the head of a heraldic beast. From this you derive both literal and metaphysical potency from this transformation. Choose one, common options include:

Falcon: Able to see great distances with extreme clarity, +1 on Navigation rolls outdoors
Crocodile: Can bite for 1d8 damage, able to hold breath for hours
Lion: Your voice carries tenfold the distance of normal men, +1 on Reaction rolls with nobility, 1d6 damage bite
Stag: +1 on attempts to sue for peace, +1 to Mental saving throws
Wolf: Can bite for 1d6 damage, exceptional sense of smell for tracking

Game-Rules/Equipment.title: Equipment
Game-Rules/Equipment.content:
A naked warrior presents nowhere near the threat as a killer in full harness. Surviving, and thriving, will often be determined by how prepared an adventurer is based on the tools at their disposal. This section details gear, statistics for weapons, and general prices.
Each piece of equipment lists a rarity and average price. These are considered relevant where trade is common, usually for cities along the Valles. For adventurers far from civilization there are no listed prices; each negotiation is its own event. A manticore may sell a dozen swords for fresh meat, while suspicious back-countrymen may have little use for gold. Where civilized trade is possible, the GM should consider the rarity when purchases are being made. If an adventurer requires equipment on short notice this may need a Charisma + Trade check based on rarity. Failure may instead require an adventure to acquire the gear, otherwise most merchants will accept a special order for triple normal price to deliver the goods next season.

Game-Rules/Magic/Rituals/Initiations/Wad.title: Wading Through the Trials of Heron
Game-Rules/Magic/Rituals/Initiations/Wad.content:
The sacred rite to Heron is traditionally administered in his great temple at Hapolis to induct new members of their mystery cult. However an ancient promise requires them to permit anyone capable of reading more than one ancient script to attempt the ritual - even enemies of the cult.
Nautilus venom is used to drive the initiate mad with thirst over the course of the blue moon, before permitting them to imbibe a psychoactive elixir brewed from their own blood. From there the initiate passes into an ephemeral realm containing a seemingly infinite library of books. Each book is 410 pages long, with unrelenting pages of 40 lines each of 80 random letters. Amidst this enormity the initiate must locate a book which contains a single coherent sentence and speak it aloud. These words themselves are then written down by the scribes to be consulted for divinatory use later.
It is a mathematical certainty that inside those vast halls lies a perfect book written by Heron himself, containing all wisdom and knowledge. Yet so vast is that realm it is said that not even the gods themselves would live long enough to find it.

Game-Rules/Magic/Spells/Adjuration/Fire/.title: Kindling the Soul
Game-Rules/Magic/Spells/Adjuration/Fire/.content:
Each Kindling of the Soul is an expression of inner, personal power, and must be tailored by the caster to their unique nature. This process of personal reflection requires at least a season; during which choose one skill, one saving throw, and one ability score.
Finally, in a decisive moment the initiate casts the ritual. Declaring their drive for personal power outside the limitations of fate or gods; and opening their soul to the primal flame.

Roll a DC 12 skill check using the chosen skill in the form of a personal challenge - failure burns away 1d6 training points from the chosen skill
Roll the saving throw as the flames consume you - failure applies a permanent -1 penalty to this save
Roll 1d20 as fire assaults you - if this number exceeds your ability score then it is reduced by 1

If at least one of these rolls succeeds then the caster has their potency in Fire increased by 1, but not over their normal maximum.

Game-Rules/Magic/Spells/Enchantment/Stab.title: Stabilize the Alchemist's Efforts
Game-Rules/Magic/Spells/Enchantment/Stab.content: Using this ritual the caster infuses a potion, elixir, or other alchemical substance with preservative energies. As a result it will remain fresh indefinitely, no longer requiring the efforts of an alchemist to maintain.

Game-Rules/Season-Phase/Seasonal-Activit.title: Seasonal Activities
Game-Rules/Season-Phase/Seasonal-Activit.content:
Seasonal procedure

Consult the fates - Only done at the start of a new year, the GM draws from the deck to see what omens will preside.
Declare seasonal activities -Each character decides what they will do for the season, discuss any possibilities for adventure.
Roll for random event - Roll 1d6, on a 1 a notable event has occurred.
Resolve events - Scenes and events unfold from any events, complications, opportunities, or natural consequences of the character’s endeavors.
Pay upkeep - Deduct upkeep and living expenses, details below.
Record outcome in chronicle - Write down the year, season, activity each character undertook, and the outcome - including training points gained, in the group’s chronicle.

Be it the storm-wracked days of Monsoon or the treacherous season of the Southern Wind, the rhythm of the seasons determines much of the life of the Shrinelands. Each season characters choose what their main undertaking will be. Below are listed a number of examples, if none fit you may always work with the GM on some sort of endeavor. Time spent this way is the main way characters gain training points, with most activities granting a specific number to the skill involved.
Adventure is a large portion of any adventurer’s life, and characters may choose to stage an expedition whenever they so choose. Most seasonal activities may continue so long as no more than fifteen days are spent away.
Most people in the Shrinelands do not lead lives of such daring and adventure, and typically spend most of their seasons working - the most basic seasonal activity. Heroes, however, should take particular note on the sections involving training and gaining a level.
If an opportunity or complication arises during a seasonal activity this may result in a situation needing to be resoled at a finer timescale to determine the outcome of the activity. Generally these are the purview of the GM to adjudicate, although the group as a whole may feel free to suggest ideas.
A complication could

have unexpected events threaten the outcome
suffer from a rival, or perhaps a minor spirit, deciding to intervene
cause the result to be different than intended, especially in the season of Chaos

An opportunity could

allow the character to strengthen a relationship during the course of the season
provide a boon on related work in the future
grant an additional bonus to the outcome

Seasonal Activities
Work
Undertake one’s profession. To do so requires the basic tools of their trade, and access to a market. Make a skill check for the sort of work done, and gain income based on the result. This is expressed in terms of a character’s typical earnings - usually 25 coins per season. Gain 1 training point in the skill used.





























WorkOutcomePoor (1-6)typical x 3/4Basic (7-9)typical incomeExceptional (10-12)typical x 1.25Masterful (13-15)typical x 1.5Legendary (16+)typical x 2
This usually takes the form of commission work, such as for Alchemy or Artisanry, but may also be day-labor for less specific skills. Characters wishing to increase their typical income will need to gain important clients, membership in a guild, or more useful facilities for their work.
Level-Up
Characters who have accrued enough experience points to advance to the next level may do so by undertaking a season of training in their unique art. During this season a character may also undertake one of their iconic endeavors, see each class for details.
At the conclusion of this season

Roll the character’s total hit dice, adding their Constitution modifier to each die roll. Use this as their new maximum hit points if it is higher than their current maximum, otherwise increase their maximum hit points by 1.
Note increases to Attacks, Leadership, Saves and other modifiers on their class chart

Study a Book
Gain deep insight from the power of the written word, however this is neither trivial nor passive. In addition to needing basic literacy, usually one rank of Lore and Language will suffice, the character will need understanding of the script the book is written in. Alongside this they must work on the skill involved. A character learning swordsmanship from a dueling manual requires a blade and sparring partner, one wishing to learn about metalwork would require some basic tools to experiment with. Multiple characters may generally all use the same tome to learn, so long as their training is occurring in tandem. If in doubt the maximum number of simultaneous students for this is the highest Wisdom modifier among prospective learners.
Each book will specify the number of training points which are gained from its use, and the number of seasons a character may benefit from the text before having consumed the entirety of its knowledge. Other books may have additional benefits, such as gaining a new skill specialty, or other perils. Record the name of the text under ‘books read’ on the character’s sheet.
Train With a Master
Characters may enlist a more skilled practitioner to teach them during a season. For skills this requires the teacher have at least one more rank in the skill than their student. Gain training points equal to 2 + teacher’s Wisdom modifier - typically 3 or 4. A teacher can perform their own seasonal activities by using the learner as an apprentice, so long as their activity is using the same skill. Teaching up to Lead + Charisma modifier students is possible, but in this case the master must dedicate their entire season to teaching.
Expertise may also be learned this way. This requires the master must have a heroic level of that expertise, and two seasons are required for the student to become an initiate. May also involve lengthy or dangerous initiation rituals which must be passed in addition to the time spent. When learning a new expertise no additional training points are gained.
Hone an Expertise
A character may spend a season in intensive understanding of an expertise they poses. Increase it to heroic level. Remember that the total number of heroic expertise a character may have depends on their level.
Heroic expertise are an ongoing lifestyle, and as such a character may choose to neglect their training if they so desire. In effect downgrading an expertise from heroic to initiate, typically done if they wish to ‘replace’ a previous heroic expertise with a newly acquired one.
Teach
See details above with Training. This activity is required when instruction more than a single apprentice. For this activity no skill roll is required, and the teacher gains a single training point in both Lead and the another training point in the subject of their course.
Practice
Characters may improve their skills through undirected practice, although this is not as effective as finding a skilled master or a useful tome. Magical skills may not be improved this way, but otherwise the character gains 2 training points.
Craft
Use Artisanry or Alchemy to produce something of value.
Research
Attempt to answer a question.
Master a New Spell
A character with access to a spell tome may attempt to master the spell contained within. Doing so requires that their rank in the magical skill be at least as high as the occlusion of the spell. A spellcaster may also teach a spell to another spellcaster, similarly requiring the student’s understanding of the given magical technique be sufficient to the occlusion.
Mastering a spell grants two training points in the corresponding magical skill.
Enchant an Item
Characters who have mastered any Enchantment spells may use them to create magic items. This requires a continual application of magical energy, during this season they will always be missing the amount of soul points required to cast the enchantment spell.
Each spell is slightly different, and may specify the particulars of the process. However generally this requires a large amount of magic essence. Gain one training point in the corresponding magical skill.
Cast a Grand Ceremony
Grand ceremonies are spells so potent they require an entire season of preparation, alignment, and magical work. Interruption may require Concentration checks to control the power involved. See the individual spells for details.
Endeavor
A catch-all for other activities not covered.#todo
Upkeep
#todo
Score
Reduced by Trade

Game-Rules/Skills.title: Skills
Game-Rules/Skills.content:
Using Skills
For situations that fall under the ordinary duties of a regular practitioner, no roll is required.
Additionally, should players come up with a suitable elegant and insightful plan, then it is not the role of the GM to enforce a skill check to sabotage this. However, many moments of tension include the possibility of failure, in this case a skill check is made.
2d6 + Skill Rank + Characteristic Modifier
If the result is greater than or equal to the difficulty then the check is a success. Most times the difficulty is known ahead of time unless there are particularly inclement or mysterious circumstances. In some situations success or failure by 2 can have moderating results.
If you roll doubles then there are additional effects. Odd numbers usually result in a complication, while even numbers offer an opportunity. Double 1’s results in a disaster. On Double 6s your effort is aided by some supernatural power, who will expect to be thanked, consult the Oracle to determine who this is.





























DifficultyGuideline-Trivial tasks, usually do not require a roll7Simple10Challenging13Master16+Legendary





















ModifierSituation+/- 1Usefully favorable or unfavorable circumstances+/- 2Highly inclement or fortuitous conditions+1Having an associated skill of at least Expert (3) rank
Sometimes a skill roll may be made with either a boon or a bane. These are usually the result of spells, active aid, or supernatural hinderance. When rolling with a boon roll an additional d6 and keep the two highest dice; a bane also rolls an additional die but instead the lower dice are kept. Boons and banes cancel each other out, possibly resulting in a roll with no additional dice. Multiple such effects stack however; so a skill check benefitting from two boons would roll a total of four dice - keeping the two highest.
Skill Rank
Track the total number of training points in each skill, these determine a character’s total skill rank. When rolling a skill check the rank is added to the result.








































Skill Ranktraining pointsTitle12Tyro26312Expert420530Master642Grandmaster
Colloquially the skill ranks have names. Characters of at least rank 3, experts, may provide aid in the form of a boon in relevant situations. Additionally for skill checks which could reasonably be covered by multiple skills, such as tracking (with bushcraft) a creature you are familiar with (via lore), you gain a +1 bonus to the roll if at least both skills are expert (3) rank.
Specializations are a focused subdomain of a particular skill. Your character is assumed to have basic competence in this area, and when applicable, your rank is considered one higher. Rogues automatically gain one specialization in each of their general and martial skills, otherwise they may be earned from certain traits or particularly insightful books. Under each skill are a list of example specializations, however these are by no means restrictive.
Artisanry, Language, Lore, and Exotic Arms are “specialized skills” and operate slightly differently. For each rank a character has in these skills they automatically gain a new specialization, however when operating outside of these areas it is often the case that they are no better off than someone without any ranks in that skill. In essence they are groups of distinct skills united under a single banner.





























































































































General SkillsMartial SkillsMystical SkillsAlchemyArcheryAdjurationAthleticsBrawlAlterationArtisanry*Exotic Arms*ConjurationBeastmasteryHand WeaponEnchantmentBushcraftGreat WeaponThaumaturgyConcentrationThrownDevicecraftDiplomacyDivinationHealInvestigationLanguage*LeadLore*MathematicsMiningNavigationPerformRitualSailSeneschalStealthTrade
General and Special Skills
Alchemy
An alchemist may extract useful materials form slain monsters, rare plants, or potent mineral substances. Each creature has a unique usage - which is not initially known to all alchemists - but the process is otherwise a simple one requiring only basic training, tools, and a few minutes of work. At the most basic this can create vials of venom from serpents, but also could include distilling its counterfactor from the blood of a mongoose. Unless you choose to use a live snake or engage in other such unwise practices there is usually no chance of failure for this process.
Alchemical goods will become spoiled, inert, hazardous, or otherwise unusable unless a skilled alchemist keeps them properly.  A character with alchemist’s tools may maintain a number of such items equal to twice their ranks in Alchemy plus their Intelligence modifier.
Additionally the alchemist may labor over the course of a season on more complex formulae. Doing so requires a recipe and the appropriate ingredients. For more details see Alchemy

























DifficultyExample-Create extracts from a fresh source7Assay the purity of gold, silver, or other known materials10Create an extract from a poor or incomplete source13Concoct a rare formulae from a formulae book
Specializations: bombs, oils, elixirs, poisons
Artisanry
Aptitude with craftsmanship, including the fabrication and appraisal of such goods. As a specialized skill a character automatically gains a specialization for each rank. However, the skill itself is not as broadly applicable - an artisan working outside their area of expertise will not be able to apply their skill rank to such efforts.
Used for crafting.

















DifficultyExample7Simple repairs in the field13Repair an exceedingly delicate object while travelling
Specializations: clockwork, jewelry, masonry, weaponsmith, armorsmith, woodwork, glasswork, weaver
Athletics
Bend bars, lift gates, and other feats of bodily prowess and Strength. When used with Dexterity one can leap between rooftops or balance on a wave-tossed ship. Used also when fleeing from battle, without a cohesive strategy to retreat it becomes a contest of either Constitution or Dexterity for direct pursuit.

























DifficultyExample7Break down a wooden door10Walk a tightrope13Swim across a perilous river- DRTake a penalty equal to armor’s damage reduction for tests of balance or flexibility
In the context of tactical combat a character may freely ignore such obstacles as chasms or difficult terrain for a number of paces equal to their ranks in Athletics, minus any damage reduction from armor.
Specializations: balance, climb, jump, marathon, swim
Bushcraft
The ability to survive in the wilderness. Includes creating basic shelters, setting snares, rigging a travois, and following tracks.





























DifficultyExample6Follow fresh tracks7Find supplies in typical terrain10Follow tracks after some weathering11Identify rare herb15Make camp during a monsoon
Specializations: herblore, tracking, survival, one particular type of terrain
Concentration
spiritual AC
Devicecraft
Aptitude at finding traps, bypassing locks, setting pitfalls, and minor acts of legerdemain and dexterity. Much of the modern use of devicecraft revolves around clockwork from New Lankh. Advanced devices may also require the use of an Artisanry specialization.
Specializations: trapfinding, pickpocketing, lockpicking
Diplomacy
War may be diplomacy by other means, but the diplomat concerns themselves with victory instead of battle. This skill covers understanding the motives of others, and persuading them of your notion of truth. Either through honest or dishonest means. While usually based on Charisma, Wisdom can be used when providing wise and honest counsel in the hopes that your interlocutor will see sense.





























DifficultyCrowd6Room of strangers8Large mob12Entire army, huge crowd-1Poor social status*Apply modifiers from Reaction rolls, up to +/- 2
Specializations: suing for peace, deception, a particular type of person such as: nobility, Alcherans, or priests
Divination
Divination is the art of interpreting dreams, signs, and omens from the gods. Alongside passive observation of the world an expert in divination is capable of using cartomancy and haruspexy to pry more intrusively into the plans of She-Who-Lurks.
As the art of divination is highly subject to the unknown, both player and GM roll 2d6 when making a divination check. The GM then chooses one of these rolls to be the result for what determines the divination. Although initially mysterious there are patterns to which is chosen.
Specializations: predicting weather, haruspex, averting disaster
Heal
Application of the medical arts of both the mind and body. Including diagnostic practices, treatment of diseases, expurgation of poisons, and general palliation. Heal checks do not directly restore hit points, however a trained Healer tending to the wounded increases how many hit points they restore based on their rank. More details are in damage and healing.
Specializations: autopsy, treating wounds, diseases
Investigation
Language
Skill at speaking the many tongues of the land, as well as reading ancient secrets. Also includes the use of codes and ciphers. All characters learn one additional language per skill rank, written down as a specialization; in addition to automatically starting with their native language.
A character with at least one rank in both Language and Lore is literate, outside of this the ability to read is not common.
Languages

Psuedophidian -

Specializations: forgery, ciphers
Lead
Ability to inspire loyalty in followers, and motivate them to direct action. If the efficacy of an ambush or loyalty of underlings would be in question a Lead check, possibly modified by Wisdom or Charisma addresses this. Notable for increasing your leadership score.
Specializations: a particular type of follower
Lore

























DifficultyExample lore6Basic familiarity with a phenomena, a good plan to learn more or find a more detailed source later8Recall an overview of a complex history10Identify a rare monster, recognize a strange essence seep14+Descent initial theory when encountering a unique and unprecedented subject
Knowledge of beasts, phenomenon, and the world at large. All sages have some knowledge of numerous fields, however as a specialized skill characters are entitled to choose one specialization per rank of Lore they have. Within a loremaster’s specialization they always know something, and if a roll is even required, are rolling to see just how deep their knowledge is. If in doubt provide a useful overview then reduce the difficulty by 2. Particularly when monster are involved, hand over a copy of their monster entry. Local variants, strange enchantments, or other complications may still be kept secret - but there is no need to be coy with a character who has specialized lore.
Suggestions for such specializations are:

Realmlore: study of the effects of dominions, auras, and beings from beyond
History: heraldry, politics, family lineages, and the origin and purpose of social structures
Death: undead, funerary rites, autopsies
Architecture
Beasts
Creatures of Chaos
Lords of Law

Others may be created as needed, however keep in mind that the specific practice and mysteries of other skills are already covered by those. Alchemy already regards substances and their uses, and each magical technique covers the knowledge of spellcraft of that type.
Navigation
Perform
Ritual
Sail
Operating watercraft of all kinds, including basic repairs.
Specializations: large ships, ropework, small ships
Seneschal
Skill required to run operate an organization, understand contracts, or operate within a bureaucracy.
Specializations: legal codes, organization
Stealth
Moving undetected, setting ambushes, and remaining unseen.
Specializations: ambush, a particular environment (urban, wilderness, desert)
Trade
The ability to make money via mercantile means. Includes appraising goods, haggling, finding valuable goods and deals.
Specializations: a particular type of good, a specific market (such as Hapolis)
Martial Skills
Martial skills represent training with different types of weapons. Most importantly these are added to attack rolls with related weapons. Specializations for martial skills are always a particular weapon within that school. Such masters of the art of combat are able to make use of the mastery properties of that weapon.
Archery
Brawl
Adds to armor class
Exotic Arms
A specialized skill that applies to unique weapons. Ranks in this skill only apply to weapons you have a specialization in.
Hand Weapon
Great Weapon
Thrown Weapon
Used to make ranged attacks with hurled weaponry. Most notable for skill at hurling bombs and using slings.
Magical Techniques
Magical techniques are covered in more detail as their pertain to performing Sorcery. The techniques known to this age are: Adjuration, Alteration, Conjuration, Enchantment, and Thaumaturgy. In addition to determining what spells can be mastered and contributing to spellcasting rolls; a technique check may be called upon to identify or understand a spell being cast or related magical phenomenon.
Minor Skills
Some professions are unlikely to be relevant for most adventurers, but are still important for the day-to-day lives of many people in the Shrinelands. In general, adventurers can probably use relevant general skills for most tasks. Skills are meant to be rather broad and powerful. However, in the event more granularity is needed you are free to invent more skills, so long as you carefully consider the negative space you are carving out of the default skill list.


                  
                  Where is the perception skill? 
                  
                
You may have notice there is no skill called something like “awareness”, “spot”, or “notice.” Such circumstances are instead related to a character’s Wisdom score.

Game-Rules/System-Overview.title: System Overview
Game-Rules/System-Overview.content:
Basic Rules Reference
The rules of Shrinelands RPG are similar in many ways to other d20 RPGs, although with a few notable differences. This section summarizes the rules and rolls required for play. Explained in more detail in the following sections.
Saving throw: roll 2d20 and add save to each, compare each to save target.

Includes mental, physical, and evasion saving throws.
Overpowering effect: only roll 1d20 and treat other as failure.
Glancing effect: only roll 1d20 and treat other as a success.
Usually attacks from creatures of double the target’s level are overpowering, while those from half the target’s level are only glancing.

Damage Reduction (DR): decrease damage taken by this amount when attacked. Only applies when character is ready for battle, exceptions include being knocked prone or taken by surprise.
Modes of Play
As the adventure proceeds players, including the GM, work together to experience the unfolding events. This means shifting between a number of time-scales based on the situation. Long-term characters train, pursue projects, and live through Seasonal Activities.
When they choose to strike out on an expedition the game becomes a matter of the events of each day while adventuring, matters of minutes plunging the depths of a dungeon, or moments of mortal import in Encounters or Combat. It is up to the choices made by the players involved which of these is used, as the GM uses these based on the circumstances the characters enter.
Skills
The GM may call for a skill check to determine the outcome of a given situation, although in many cases a sufficiently well-articulated and considered plan may render this unnecessary. Each skill check also has an associated Characteristic - such as Strength to bend bars or Wisdom to perform first aid. To make a skill check roll  2d6 + Skill Rank + Characteristic modifier. Rolling doubles on this check results in a complication for an odd number, or an opportunity for an even number. More details are in Skills.
Characters gain training points in each skill, which then increases in rank once the next threshold is reached. 2 training points for rank one, 6 for rank two, 12 for rank three, 20 for rank four, and 30 for rank five.
Hit Points and Damage
The Shrinelands is a place of vast beauty but also mortal peril, typically tracked by the loss of hit points. Each character has a maximum and current number of hit points, when taking damage reduce your character’s current hit points.
When this reaches 0 additional damage, including that from the attack which reduced HP to 0, is instead dealt as damage to the character’s Constitution characteristic. For example, a character with 4 hit points and 11 Constitution suffers a 7 damage blow from a manticore - now that character would have 0 hit points and only 8 Constitution. A character reduced to 0 Constitution dies, with the exception of those heroic figures who have class levels. Such exceptional individuals may take a number of points of damage equal to their level beyond this and still survive, so a third level adventurer will not die until their Constitution reaches -4. Otherwise, most average individuals can be treated as incapacitated or deceased when their hit points reach 0.
Anytime a character loses Constitution due to damage they must make a roll on behalf of the lord of the underworld as he tries to claim their frail mortal form. To do so roll 1d20 and roll for doom, with especially disastrous results occurring if the number is twice or more their now reduced Constitution. Details of wounds are covered later in the chapter.

























Roll for DoomResult20Instantly incapacitated, major wound, and will die if not treatedDouble ConstitutionMajor woundAbove ConstitutionModerate woundLess than ConstitutionNo additional effect, beyond the looming threat of mortality
Characters generally regain 1 hit point per day of rest, usually meaning that eventually adventurers must return to a safe harbor to heal. Damage to characteristics, such as Constitution, is much slower to heal. Each season a character regains half, rounded up, of the amount they are missing in each characteristic. During this time they may wish to pursue Seasonal Activities.
Saving Throws
When subject to a spell, falling rocks, or other unexpected circumstances a character may attempt to avoid the worst via a saving throw.

Physical saving throw: resist poison, disease, transformation magic, harsh environments
Evasion saving throw: avoid explosion, falling rocks
Mental saving throw: hypnotic gazes, mental magic, possession

Rolling a save involves rolling two d20s and adding the corresponding save modifier to each. Situations involving weak hazards typically require a total of 10 or higher for a success, while a strong hazard requires a 15 or higher. Generally if both rolls succeed then the character suffers almost no ill effects. Two failures results in the worst possible outcome, typically fully damage. One failure and one success is, as expected, a more intermediate result.
Some effects can be either overpowering or glancing. When an effect is produced by a character of twice your level it is overpowering, while those from characters half or less are glancing. In these cases only roll a single die for a saving throw, the other result is automatically determined - a failure in the overpowering case and an automatic success should it be glancing.
In play this means as a moderate level sorcerer an attempt to influence lesser minds, those who are half your level, will always result in some effect - with the target rolling a save against your overpowering spell to do their best to mitigate its full force.
Spellcasting
Characters may cast any spell they have mastered by spending soul points. Each spell is associated with one of the elements: air, earth, fire, water, celestial - and the cost of the spell depends on how its magnitude compares to the degree of elemental Attunement that character has. Casting a spell which has a magnitude equal to their Attunement costs 12 soul points. Having an Attunement one greater reduces the cost to 6, with further Attunement resulting in costs of 3 and finally 1.
Characters may make use of the environment to further ease and enhance spellcasting. Even something as small as a Fire mage carrying a torch has a subtle effect, but most would prefer to work magic inside a caldera. See Sorcery for more.
Combat
For full scale skirmishes the Combat procedure is used.
Rule Appendix
Wounds
Elemental Resistance
Ignore the highest X dice of damage, so a creature with 2 fire resistance taking 5d4 fire damage would only take the lower 3.

Game-Rules/Welcome-to-the-Shrinelands.title: Welcome to the Shrinelands
Game-Rules/Welcome-to-the-Shrinelands.content:
It is I, his chronicler, who alone can tell thee of his saga. Let me tell you of the days of high adventure!


Welcome to the Shrinelands, the sun-baked cradle of the world. North of the wine-dark waters of the Valles, east of dread Noctis, south of fallen Tharsis, and west of the world!
This particular saga concerns the fate of the Tower of Madness, a mystical fastness you have been invited to take ownership of - save for the perils of the tower and the land surrounding.
This is a game about sword and sorcery in a mythological age, where players take the roles of adventures, leaders, and wizards to experience how their life unfolds. Play proceeds on varying timescales: moment by moment in tense battle, minute by minute when creeping through unknown ruins, day by day exploring the vast wilderness north of the Valles, and season by season as characters learn new spells, train, and build their influence.
Below are details on creating a character, and a summary of some key differences from similar fantasy adventure games.
Seasonal Activities

most training points gained by studying during seasons  - perhaps from a wise mentor or an ancient tome
grand rituals take time to cast, such as the Kindling the Soul - others curse the land itself or summon potent allies
each year harvests are brought in, hirelings paid, fortifications rise and fall - your reputation and influence can be of equal value to any coin or gem

Years may be required, as a game using a paradigm more similar to sandbox style play there will be many challenges which are insurmountable in the moment. Any enemy fortress may well be impregnable without returning with more allies, new magic, knowledge of a hidden passage, or time spent subverting one of their watch masters to your cause.
Exploration

game takes place over a large hexmap - with special attention paid to the challenges of travel, expenditure of supplies, and discovering the vast region of the Shrinelands

Leaders of Men

gain a Leadership score - in pitched battles powerful adventurers are accompanied by bodyguards, squads of archers, or even tamed beasts

Adventurers from the Shrinelands

characters and character options are specific to the world of the Shrinelands
classes are a baseline, not a limitation - most training points are gained based on your characters choices, a class is more of a guarantee of competency in a given domain than a restriction

Play is similar to many other fantasy adventure games, with a few key differences. Below is something of a “strategy guide” to understand the themes and options available.
Being a Rogue
Rogues are those who survive by their wits, expertise, and the favor of the gods. When gaining training points rogues gain one more than they would otherwise. Because of this they benefit from a diverse education, and should be keen to seek out potential mentors or manuals. Both of those allow a character who spends a season in study to gain a number of training points based on their quality. Alongside this all characters gain free training points based on their Intelligence modifier each year, something which the rogue can easily take advantage of.
Also, there are no re-rolls other than a rogue’s ability to re-roll a skill check once per scene - which can often be the turning point for major events. A good rogue should feel free to take bold action, knowing that often the gods will protect them.
Odysseys is a prime example of a rogue, and many more archetypes than one may initially assume fall under this banner. Diplomats, priests, alchemists, healers, dilettantes - all ways to embrace the gifts granted you.
Being a Warrior
Warriors are those destined for greatness on the field of honor. They also have the highest base leadership of the classes - often being on the path from barbarian to king. While having high martial skills is obviously a boon, warriors should not feel limited to any single skill. With their natural aptitude for combat picking up incidental skill in other combat styles will increase the ranges they are effective at.
Alongside this Teach and Lead can be useful for a warrior wishing to train and lead an elite squad.
Being a Wizard
Magic is a unique expression of the nature of the Shrinelands. Each spell is a combination of one of the schools of magic, and a source of power. A given magic-user will likely only have mastery over 2 or 3 of these elements - meaning there will be much magic that a fire mage can perform that an air mage cannot.
Being from the Shrinelands
The Adventure Begins
Strategy Guide
The Hypeurus Age
An age of bronze and blood

Shrinelands/Ephemeral-Realm/Gods/Minor/A.title: Asterion
Shrinelands/Ephemeral-Realm/Gods/Minor/A.content:
Holy Days
High Holy Days

12th of Law Season: Triumph of Asterion - during this day a great feast is held along with the largest of the Labyrinth Games. On this day all who defend their home gain a +2 attack bonus

Minor Holy Days

12th of Monsoon, Chaos, and Dry Seasons - each of these days a lesser Labyrinth Game is held, and is considered an auspicious occasion to train for battle.

Cult of Mighty Asterion
Cult Activities
Labyrinth Games
On each of the holy days of Asterion the cult hosts a Labyrinth Game. During these a stone maze is constructed to hold a number of cultic treasures, and defended by both current members and the spirits of deceased members. All are welcome to participate, and most events are conducted with a spirit of fun and camaraderie.
Those seeking Master level membership must find at least one of the relics of Asterion as proof of their commitment. However, there is also a deeper secret. Far below the public labyrinth is a greater maze in which is hidden Asterion’s own Ax of Rulership. It is only on this day that the ax becomes vulnerable, and the greatest of the god’s protections are devoted to this. A seeker who enters this lower level will not find a festival-day game, but rather the deadly ire of the cult’s most seasoned warriors.
Members of the Cult of Mighty Asterion
Lay Members

50 coin per year membership
Must attend at least one function per year
Swear to defend Hapolis in times of need

Many citizens of Hapolis are lay members of the Cult of Mighty Asterion. This forms a loose militia should the city need defending, but otherwise is a large social club. Non-citizens are permitted membership at this level, although the prohibition against weapons atop the acropolis makes this somewhat complicated.
Initiation only requires payment of the membership fee, vouching from a member of at least initiate status, and participation in one of the Labyrinth Games.
Benefits

Gain 2 Reputation points with cult
Half cost on training in Navigation, Great Weapon, and Mining

Shrinelands/Objects/Devices/Astrolabe.title: Astrolabe
Shrinelands/Objects/Devices/Astrolabe.content:
Astrolabe
Elaborate brass mechanism for measuring the stars and land. User can always tell their latitude down to the hexleague, and permits accurate estimation of distances to visible landmarks. Includes also the capabilities of a compass.

Days are numbered from 1 to 451, and tracked rather assiduously even by ordinary people. While it is common if asked for the date to be simply told “the 123rd of this year” terms such as “mid-season” are also just as common.
Being equatorial the Shrinelands are nearly always hot, with instead seasons being divided up differently than those of your typical world. Each year stars with an intercalary period of 11 days called Still, reserved for preparations for the new year and special holidays. Following this are five unequal seasons divided in to 40 day months, with each season named after the wind which tends to dominate.

East Season: the wind of Chaos, a time of fickle weather and rampant growth, although largely temperate
North-East Season: usually called monsoon season, each year brings incredibly downpours only interrupted by the occasional hurricane
North Season: dominated by the wind of misfortune. This season is oppressively hot, oft plagued by sandstorms from the cursed desert
West Season: the winds of Law bring a welcome relief from the heat. Generally cooler, most farmers use this as a second growing season, while others use it to march to war.
South Season: relatively dry and warm, home to few extremes although prone to bring the unexpected

Every 22 years after the Wandering Moon visits the world the duration of a year changes. After the moon has shown its bright side the year is longer for the next cycle. During these “long years” there is an extra season, Winter. Winter is still nowhere near as punishing as it is in other regions, but is the only time snow is ever seen in the Shrinelands.
Three Moons
The Red Moon
The red moon, also known as the Herald of War, travels across the sky opposite the direction of the sun multiple times per day, dividing up the day into a ‘watch.’ Each watch is about a third of a day, with 4 hours where the moon is visible followed by 4 hours where it isn’t present in the sky.
This can lead to relatively frequent partial eclipses during some portions of the year, notable more closer to autumn and winter. Because the cycle of the red moon does not precisely divide the day in three the exact time of moonrise gradually shifts. Longer periods of time are divided by when sunrise happens while the red moon is visible, “red days,” and those where it is not.
The Blue Moon
The mystic moon hangs in the sky for days at a time, and is much smaller than the red moon, only barely discernable as more than a large star. These cycles take about five and a half days.
The Wandering Moon
An ill-omened moon which arrives but once every 22 years.

Shrinelands/Time/Seasons/Chaos-Season.title: Chaos Season
Shrinelands/Time/Seasons/Chaos-Season.content:
Chaos season is home to intermittent changestorms, odd whirlwinds of magic that sweep across the land. From these descend bolts of change, twisting trees and bringing life to whatever is struck across the land. The very desperate sometimes wander unprotected into these storms, hoping that any life that Chaos grants them would be better than what they have now.
Changestorm
Bolts of change leave behind never before seen animals, split into evil twin, leave veins of gold
Turn hair different color, switch minds, turn trees into eels, change class

Shrinelands/Time/Times-of-Note/Divinatio.title: Divination Day
Shrinelands/Time/Times-of-Note/Divinatio.content:
The first day of Law season and the first day of the year. All eyes turn westward to see if ash spews from the mountains of Tharsis. A clear day heralds a good year, but the dread ash is considered a poor omen.
During this time diviners are consulted for matters about the upcoming year. Those who wish to can attempt a grand haruspex, although demand for pure animals is high - possibly costing upwards of 50 coins.
